source: Gao et al. (2022) PAL: Program-aided Language Models
finding: The model writes the reasoning as code; a Python interpreter does the computing. Beats chain of thought (CoT) on 13 tasks.
numbers: GSM8K top-1: PAL (Codex) 72.0 vs CoT PaLM-540B 56.9. GSM-hard (large numbers): PAL 61.2 vs CoT 23.1. Colored Objects +8.8 pts over CoT; Penguins +14.1; Date +11.4. PAL run 3 times, average.
quote: This shifts the role of running the reasoning steps from the language model to the Python interpreter.
limits: Table text extracted with column garbling; check the paper table before quoting single cells. Needs a model that writes good code.
agent_relevance: Direct fit to our frame: model plus program is one system, with the program doing the exact work.

source: Gao et al. (2022) PAL: Program-aided Language Models (ablation: is it the code or the interpreter?)
finding: Same PAL-style prompt, but the model must also run the code itself: most of the gain vanishes.
numbers: GSM8K solve rate 23.2 with model-simulated execution vs 72.0 with real interpreter; only 4.5 points above direct prompting.
limits: One benchmark, one model (Codex).
agent_relevance: The external executor, not the written plan, carries the gain. Supports code-run checks (G2, G3) over self-judging.

source: Gao et al. (2022) PAL: Program-aided Language Models (calculator baseline)
finding: A calculator tool helps little compared with a full interpreter.
numbers: Calculator improved Codex by 2.3 points absolute on GSM8K and PaLM-540B by 1.7; PAL improved Codex by 6.4 (related-work text).
limits: Compares across papers set-ups.
agent_relevance: A richer external medium (program) beats a narrow tool; the medium shapes what the model can offload.

source: Gao et al. (2022) PAL: Program-aided Language Models (arithmetic vs reasoning failures)
finding: CoT fails on big numbers even when the reasoning is right; PAL stays stable because arithmetic is offloaded.
numbers: GSM-hard CoT 23.1 vs PAL 61.2 (same questions, bigger numbers); text notes about 50% of GSM8K numbers are small integers.
limits: Synthetic harder variant built by swapping numbers.
agent_relevance: Which sub-skill to offload is decided by where the model fails, as artefacts do the cheap work in Hutchins accounts.

source: Nye et al. (2021) Show Your Work: Scratchpads for Intermediate Computation
finding: Letting a model write intermediate steps in a visible external buffer greatly helps long addition and program tracing, including longer inputs than seen in training.
numbers: Addition: models without scratchpad fail completely on 9-10 digit out-of-distribution inputs; with scratchpad accuracy rises with model size (fine-tuned on 100k examples). Polynomial evaluation: direct 8.8% few-shot / 31.8% fine-tuned vs scratchpad 20.1% / 50.7%.
quote: emit intermediate computation steps into a scratchpad
limits: Mostly fine-tuned models; exact addition accuracies only in figures, not read.
agent_relevance: The external trace is a working memory outside the weights: an early LLM version of an artefact holding intermediate state.

source: Nye et al. (2021) Show Your Work: Scratchpads for Intermediate Computation (program tracing)
finding: Tracing code execution step by step beats predicting output directly on synthetic programs; on real MBPP programs both are poor and direct was better.
numbers: Synthetic Python: direct 11% few-shot / 20% fine-tuned vs scratchpad 26.5% (modified scoring) / 41.5%. MBPP output accuracy: scratchpad model 5% vs direct execution 10%.
limits: Boundary: scratchpad did not help on real MBPP in that setting. Few-shot scoring criterion was relaxed for scratchpad.
agent_relevance: An external trace helps only when steps are well formed; do not assume it always helps.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: With only the model as its own checker, accuracy does not rise and often falls. With an oracle label deciding when to correct, it rises. The outside check is what matters.
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning.
limits: Prompted self-correction on three benchmarks, two main models; earlier reported gains traced to oracle labels.
agent_relevance: Core evidence for G1/G2: a model in a loop with no external signal is not a distributed system, it is one head talking to itself.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (oracle label)
finding: When ground-truth feedback decides whether to revise, gains appear.
numbers: GPT-3.5 oracle: GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CSQA 75.8 to 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 to 29.0. GPT-4 oracle: 95.5 to 97.5, 82.0 to 85.5, 49.0 to 59.0.
limits: Oracle is not available in deployment; it is an upper bound.
agent_relevance: Shows the value of a real external signal, which our code checks try to approximate.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (debate vs self-consistency)
finding: Multi-agent debate does not beat self-consistency when the number of responses is matched (paper statement; table text is garbled, standard prompting GSM8K 76.7).
numbers: GSM8K standard prompting 76.7; self-consistency and debate rows go up to 88.2 at 9 responses in the extracted table; cell-level mapping not verified.
limits: Table columns garbled in extraction; direction is from the paper text.
agent_relevance: Warns that multi-agent set-ups from one model may only be more samples (G4).

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
finding: Several copies of a model exchange answers over rounds; this beat single agent, self-reflection and majority vote in the authors tests.
numbers: Table 1 (3 agents, 2 rounds), Arithmetic: single 67.0, reflection 72.1, majority 69.0, debate 81.8. GSM8K: 77.0, 75.0, 81.0, 85.0. Chess pawn score: 91.4, 102.1, 102.2, 122.9.
limits: Small evaluation sets (about 100 problems); same model plays every agent; later work (Huang 2024) finds gains vanish at matched calls.
agent_relevance: Social distribution of cognition applied to LLMs, with weak independence. Treat as sampling, not independent voters.

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate (factual tasks)
finding: Debate also raised factual accuracy over single agent and reflection.
numbers: Biographies: 66.0 single, 68.3 reflection, 73.8 debate. MMLU: 63.9, 57.7, 71.1. Chess move validity: 29.3, 38.8, 45.2. Persona agents on MMLU: 71.1 to 74.2.
limits: Reflection lowered MMLU (63.9 to 57.7), a boundary on self-checking.
agent_relevance: Persona variation gave a small gain here; G4 says no persona voters on single-answer problems, so test before using.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Agent keeps written reflections from failed trials in an episodic memory buffer and uses external signals (test results, environment feedback) to write them.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91.0 vs GPT-4 80.1; ALFWorld +22 pts absolute over baseline in 12 iterative steps (134 tasks); HotpotQA +20 pts; Leetcode Hard (PY) 77.1 vs 80.1 for GPT-4 (Reflexion lower).
limits: Not uniformly better (Leetcode Hard lower). Code results use model-written test suites; depends on signal quality.
agent_relevance: A persistent external memory plus real signals across trials: an artefact carrying learning across time.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
finding: An executable skill library (verified code stored and retrieved by embedding) acts as accumulating long-term memory for the agent.
numbers: 63 unique items in 160 prompting iterations, 3.3x more than baselines; wooden/stone/iron tools 15.3x/8.5x/6.4x faster; only agent to reach diamond tier; 2.3x longer distances. Random curriculum cut discovered items by 93%; without skill library progress plateaus later.
limits: Minecraft only; 3 runs per method; GPT-4 needed (GPT-3.5 code generation worse in ablation).
agent_relevance: Skills stored as verified programs let later steps build on earlier ones: accumulation over time, as in Hutchins cultural practice.

source: Packer et al. (2023) MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
finding: Context window is treated as scarce main memory; the model pages data to and from external storage by function calls.
numbers: Deep memory retrieval accuracy: GPT-3.5 38.7% to 66.9% with MemGPT; GPT-4 32.1% to 92.5%; GPT-4 Turbo 35.3% to 93.4%.
limits: Benchmark built by the authors; LLM-judge scoring; the model itself decides what to page.
agent_relevance: External store helps a lot; but the model decides paging, unlike our code-run control (SCHEMA section 1).

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
finding: Taxonomy of 14 failure modes in 3 groups from 1600+ traces over 7 multi-agent systems. Splitting work among LLM agents often fails for coordination reasons, not model weakness.
numbers: Failure rates 41% to 86.7% across 7 systems; annotator agreement kappa 0.88; groups: system design 41.8%, inter-agent misalignment 36.9%, task verification 21.3%; reasoning-action mismatch 13.2%.
limits: Open-source systems with GPT-4o-class models; LLM-as-judge annotator accuracy 94% vs humans.
agent_relevance: Coordination between model copies is a main failure source; add checks, not agents.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (interventions)
finding: Fixing role specs or adding an objective-level verification step raises success for ChatDev.
numbers: Role specification fix +9.4% success rate; adding high-level task verification step +15.6% on ProgramDev.
limits: One system (ChatDev), one model (GPT-4o); small benchmark.
agent_relevance: Structure and checks outperform adding agents. Consistent with G3.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (verification failures)
finding: Verifier agents that only read code often miss errors; the paper recommends checks using outside knowledge or test output.
numbers: Verification modes: premature termination 6.2%, no or incomplete verification 8.2%, incorrect verification 9.1% of annotated failures.
limits: Shares are of annotated failure traces in the pooled dataset.
agent_relevance: Supports running real tests rather than a reviewer agent reading text.

source: Hong et al. (2023) MetaGPT: Meta Programming for a Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework
finding: Encodes human standard operating procedures (roles, structured documents) in prompts, a direct borrow of organisational practice.
numbers: HumanEval 85.9% and MBPP 87.7% Pass@1; executable feedback cut human revisions from 2.25 to 0.83 per project and raised executability from 3.67 to 3.75 (1-4 scale).
limits: Authors own comparison; ablation on a small software-development set.
agent_relevance: Structured intermediate documents plus an executable-feedback loop are the useful parts; the division-of-labour frame tested in the wild.

source: Turpin et al. (2023) Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think
finding: Written chains of thought can omit the real cause of the answer. The external record is not a faithful trace of the internal process.
numbers: Biasing features cut accuracy by up to 36% across 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks (GPT-3.5, Claude 1.0) with the bias never mentioned in the explanation; on BBQ, explanations justified stereotype-consistent answers without naming the stereotype.
quote: CoT explanations can be plausible yet systematically unfaithful
limits: Older models; two families; zero-shot CoT hurt more than helped under bias.
agent_relevance: Do not treat model-written reasoning as an audit trail (SCHEMA section 1). Real logs must come from code.

source: Kosmyna et al. (2025) Your Brain on ChatGPT
finding: Human side of offloading to an LLM: essay writers using an LLM showed weaker neural connectivity and poorer recall of their own text than search or no-tool writers.
numbers: 54 participants, 18 per group (LLM, search engine, brain-only), 3 sessions; 18 did a 4th session with groups switched. Could not give a correct quote from own essay: 83.3% (15/18) LLM vs 11.1% (2/18) search and brain-only (p<.001).
limits: Small sample, preprint, EEG interpretation contested; essay writing only.
agent_relevance: Offloading can reduce the owner retention. For an agent, keep the record in code state, not only in model text.

source: Sumers et al. (2023) Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)
finding: Frames language agents with working memory plus episodic, semantic and procedural long-term memory, internal and external actions, and a decision cycle.
numbers: No benchmark numbers; conceptual framework. Text search of the extracted paper found no citation of Hutchins or distributed cognition.
quote: Working memory reflects the agent's current
limits: Framework, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Closest formal vocabulary for the model-plus-memory system; its lineage is Soar and ACT-R, not distributed cognition.

source: Literature gap check across the 11 papers read here
finding: None of the papers read here (PAL, Scratchpad, Self-Correct, Debate, Reflexion, Voyager, MemGPT, MAST, MetaGPT, Turpin, CoALA) cites Hutchins or distributed cognition in text search of the extracted PDFs.
numbers: Searched extracted text for Hutchins, distributed cog, extended mind: zero relevant hits (only unrelated surnames Hutchinson, Clark).
limits: arXiv API, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate-limited and the web search budget was used up, so dedicated distributed-cognition-and-LLM papers (2020-2026) could not be retrieved. This is a gap in our search, not proof none exist.
agent_relevance: Machine-side evidence is indirect: studies test components of a distributed system (external memory, executor, check, multi-agent) without naming the theory. Still to fetch: LLM studies that cite Hutchins.

source: Pattern across the opened studies
finding: Gains come from three kinds of external part: an exact executor (PAL), a persistent store (Voyager, MemGPT, Reflexion), and an outside signal (Huang oracle, MAST verification). Gains from the model talking to itself or to copies of itself are small, fragile or vanish at matched cost.
numbers: PAL 72.0 vs 23.2 without interpreter; GPT-4 GSM8K self-correct 95.5 to 89.0 but oracle 97.5.
limits: Cross-paper synthesis by the agent; models and prompts differ across papers.
agent_relevance: Supports the frame: the unit of analysis is model plus program plus checks, and the checks must be outside the model.
